strengths: Clear motivation combining benefits of Gaussian and simplex diffusion through distance-based latent space representation

Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 elegantly connects distance and embedding space optimization for efficient training; Appendix C rigorously proves distance-based space generalizes simplex diffusion
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 seq-to-seq tasks with fair comparison using identical architecture and hyperparameters for embedding/simplex baselines
Significant efficiency gains: 2-10× fewer denoising steps than competing diffusion methods while maintaining quality
Consistent improvements over both embedding-based and simplex-based diffusion baselines (best mean rank among diffusion methods in Table 5)
Thorough implementation details in appendices with promised code release; good ablation on noise variance δ̃ demonstrating quality-diversity tradeoff
Honest acknowledgment and discussion of limitations (frozen embeddings, fixed sequence length) in Appendix A
weaknesses: Frozen pre-trained BERT embeddings fundamentally limit scalability and cap performance ceiling; end-to-end training not explored despite acknowledged benefits, making approach incompatible with modern scaling trends
Modest empirical improvements (typically 1-4 points) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; unclear if gains are meaningful given margins
Missing human evaluation despite making generation quality claims; automatic metrics alone insufficient for assessing text generation quality in seq-to-seq tasks

Contradictory results on Quasar-T where simplex diffusion (19.5 BLEU) outperforms SMOOTHIE (19.0 BLEU), contradicting central claims about distance-based space benefits; paper dismisses as 'architectural choice' without investigation

Non-Markovian forward process (Eq. 3) lacks adequate justification; unconventional conditioning on D₀ rather than sequential diffusion not compared against Markovian alternative or theoretically analyzed
Incremental novelty: primarily represents new latent space combining existing ideas (embeddings + semantic similarity + diffusion) without fundamental methodological innovation
Incomplete baseline comparisons: results for most methods taken from prior work [25] rather than re-implemented; only embedding and simplex redone; hyperparameter tuning procedures not detailed
Autoregressive baselines (BART, FLAN-T5) consistently outperform SMOOTHIE by substantial margins (4-8+ points), limiting practical impact

Design choices appear empirical rather than principled (e.g., MSE vs cross-entropy 'led to inferior performance' without systematic investigation; fixed noise schedule hyperparameters lack justification)

strengths: Clear motivation: The paper articulates well why existing approaches (Gaussian vs. simplex diffusion) have complementary limitations and presents a reasonable approach to combine their strengths.
Theoretical contribution: Formal analysis showing simplex diffusion is a special case of distance-based diffusion (Theorem 4.1, Appendix C) provides theoretical grounding.
Comprehensive experimental framework: Fair controlled comparison across latent spaces (distance, embedding, simplex) with identical architectures; four seq2seq tasks with detailed ablations.
Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges pre-trained embeddings, fixed sequence length, and other constraints affecting the method.
Good presentation: Generally clear writing with intuitive figures and detailed implementation details for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Mixed and task-dependent empirical results: Performance is inconsistent—SMOOTHIE underperforms simplex on Quasar-T (62.4 vs 63.0 BS) and substantially lags SeqDiffuSeq on Newsela-Auto (19.9 vs 37.1 BLEU). Strong claims of superiority are not consistently supported.

Unfair experimental comparisons: Baselines from prior work are compared alongside the authors' own implementations, introducing confounds. The authors' simplex implementation even outperforms TESS (same method), suggesting implementation differences matter.

Critical unaddressed limitation—fixed pre-trained embeddings: Uses frozen BERT embeddings; prior work ([27], [13], [25]) performs end-to-end training. This severely constrains performance and fairness of comparison, yet the paper dismisses this as future work.

Questionable core assumption: Entire approach relies on Euclidean semantic space hypothesis without empirical validation. Modern embeddings may not follow this assumption, and no ablation explores robustness to different metrics.
Lack of statistical rigor: No significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs. Reported differences could be within noise.
Limited novelty: Core contribution is applying standard Gaussian diffusion to a different latent space representation—incremental over existing diffusion variants.

Insufficient analysis of efficiency claims: Claims '2-10× fewer steps' but Table 6 shows task-dependent improvement—Quasar-T plateaus at 100 steps, XSum improves to 500 steps. No wall-clock time comparisons.
No analysis of task-dependent performance: Why does SMOOTHIE excel on XSum/QQP but fail on Newsela-Auto? When and why should practitioners use this method versus alternatives?

Theoretically sound with elegant theoretical contributions (Theorem 4.1 showing equivalence to embedding prediction; simplex as special case relationship)
Rigorous experimental methodology: fair re-implementation of embedding and simplex baselines under identical conditions; comprehensive evaluation across 4 diverse seq2seq tasks with multiple metrics
Practical efficiency improvements requiring 2-10× fewer denoising steps than competitors
Comprehensive ablations and analysis (δ̃ tuning, decoder choice, step count sensitivity)
Strong reproducibility: code promised, detailed hyperparameters, complete implementation details
Excellent presentation with clear exposition and effective visualizations (Figure 1)
weaknesses: Pre-trained embeddings limitation inadequately addressed: method relies on fixed BERT embeddings without exploring end-to-end training, contradicting claims in related work that this improves results
MSE loss choice over cross-entropy unjustified: authors claim superiority without providing ablation or evidence; this critical design choice is not experimentally validated

Inconsistent task-specific improvements: simplex outperforms on Quasar-T (19.5 vs 19.0 BLEU); SeqDiffuSeq and DiffuSeq substantially outperform on Newsela-Auto; lacks analysis of when/why semantic-aware diffusion helps
Limited scope of comparisons: all models trained from scratch (~100M params); FLAN-T5 substantially outperforms (72.7 vs 68.0 BERTScore); no comparison with pre-trained diffusion models
Semantic distance assumption underexplored: method relies on Euclidean semantic space hypothesis without analyzing failure cases, sensitivity, or justifying choice over alternative metrics
Fundamental limitation with fixed sequence length and padding inefficiency acknowledged but unaddressed
Self-conditioning shows only marginal gains despite substantial improvements in related work; deserves investigation
Hyperparameter sensitivity: δ̃ requires task-specific tuning; σ_t schedule parameters lack justification; generalization properties unclear
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided for performance differences
Technical novelty is incremental: extends image domain heat dissipation to text; core Euclidean distance-based representation is straightforward

strengths: Well-motivated approach that clearly identifies and addresses limitations of existing diffusion-based text generation methods (Gaussian vs. simplex diffusion trade-offs)
Solid theoretical contributions including Theorem 4.1 and proof that simplex diffusion is a special case of the distance-based approach (Appendix A)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 diverse datasets (unconditional and multiple seq2seq tasks) with fair comparisons under identical training conditions
Thorough ablation studies covering key components (δ̃, noise scheduler, embedding choices, self-conditioning, denoising steps) with detailed hyperparameters and reproducibility information
Consistent improvements over diffusion-based baselines across all evaluated tasks, demonstrating robustness of the approach
Multiple evaluation metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, diversity, MAUVE) appropriate for different task types and comprehensive supplementary experiments
weaknesses: Core novel contribution (sampling scheme in Eq. 9) lacks theoretical justification—authors acknowledge 'a deeper theoretical understanding remains an open question' and rely on speculative hypothesis about sparse data distributions

Computational complexity inadequately addressed: despite claims of O(batch_size × seq_len × d × V) complexity, generation is 1.75× slower than embedding diffusion; proposed solutions (clustering, top-k) dismissed as 'too complex' without implementation

Reliance on fixed pre-trained embeddings (BERT) is limiting: acknowledging this 'may hold back generation quality,' authors defer end-to-end learning to future work; Appendix F shows 80.7→36.8 MAUVE drop with GloVe embeddings

Improvements are marginal and lack statistical validation: Quasar-T shows 63.1 vs 63.0 (simplex), XSum shows 68.8 vs 68.2 (embedding); no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-run significance tests provided

Noise scheduler design (arctan with multiple hyperparameters) appears ad-hoc; Appendix H shows sensitivity to parameter d (74.2→80.7→76.5→68.9 MAUVE); limited justification versus alternative schedulers
Broader applicability claimed (graphs, protein sequences) but only text generation demonstrated; generalizability to non-text domains remains theoretical

Missing analyses: no error analysis comparing failure modes, no statistical significance testing, no ablation on vocabulary size effects, limited exploration of when/why semantic distance assumption fails

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying fundamental tradeoffs between Gaussian and simplex diffusion approaches, with effective visual intuition (Figure 1)
Solid theoretical contributions including Theorem 4.1 (elegant justification for training-sampling mismatch) and formal demonstration that simplex diffusion is a special case
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 datasets with careful reimplementation of baselines under identical conditions and extensive ablation studies
Thorough reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and dataset information enabling future work
Thoughtful technical design including custom noise scheduler and novel sampling solver (Eq. 9) demonstrating careful engineering
weaknesses: Limited novelty: distance-based token representation is a natural, straightforward extension of existing simplex diffusion; core contribution is incremental despite building on solid prior work (Rissanen et al., 2023)
Modest empirical improvements without statistical significance testing (XSum: +0.6, QQP: +0.5, Quasar-T: +1.1 BERTScore), making it unclear if differences are meaningful rather than noise
Computational cost substantially higher than embedding-based diffusion (1.75× slower, O(batch×seq_len×d×V) operations) with no serious proposed solutions, undermining practical utility

Fundamental limitation of requiring frozen BERT embeddings with no successful end-to-end training; Appendix F shows GloVe embeddings drastically underperform (36.8 MAUVE), indicating critical but unresolved dependency

Lacks theoretical justification for why distance-based smoothing preserves semantics better than embedding diffusion; semantic degradation example (Table 13) shows only approximate decodings via round-trip inference

Multiple task-specific hyperparameters (δ̃: 0.1 vs 1.1, d: 5-7) require careful tuning, reducing generality; sampling solver improvement (Eq. 9) over DDPM is marginal (68.8 vs 68.5) and mechanistically unexplained
Overclaiming in abstract regarding superiority; marked improvements on ROCStories unexplained while other tasks show <2-point gains; no analysis of when/why method succeeds or fails
Missing critical experimental rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars despite marginal improvements; unclear if reimplemented baselines represent optimal implementations

strengths: Well-motivated approach that elegantly resolves the trade-off between semantic preservation (Gaussian) and discrete preservation (simplex) diffusion by representing tokens as distance vectors
Solid theoretical foundation with rigorous proofs (Theorem 4.1, connection to generalized simplex diffusion in Appendix A) and proper variational inference framework

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with fair comparisons—embedding and simplex baselines trained under identical conditions with only latent space varied, showing consistent improvements of SMOOTHIE across multiple datasets
Exceptionally thorough ablation studies covering ñδ parameter, solvers, denoising steps, noise scheduling, self-conditioning, and embedding types, demonstrating deep understanding of design choices
Novel sampling strategy (Eq. 9) showing consistent empirical improvements with reasonable theoretical motivation regarding sparse text embedding distributions
Excellent presentation with clear writing, intuitive visualizations (Figure 1), and well-structured algorithms that effectively communicate the method
Practical considerations addressed with computational analysis, honest discussion of why straightforward approximations fail, and detailed implementation hyperparameters
weaknesses: Reliance on frozen pre-trained BERT embeddings rather than end-to-end learning, limiting adaptability; while authors explain training instability issues, this remains a significant constraint on the approach
Computational efficiency concern: 1.75× slower than embedding diffusion (Table 2) with O(batch_size × seq_len × d × V) complexity; no clear solution as approximate methods (top-k) are inadequate
Marginal improvements on key benchmarks: TEncDM outperforms SMOOTHIE on XSum (69.9 vs 68.8); Simplex achieves nearly identical performance on Quasar-T (63.0 vs 63.1); improvements dataset-dependent
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity with task-specific tuning required (ñδ varies between 0.1 and 1.1); noise scheduler parameter d causes large performance variation (68.9-80.7 MAUVE range)

Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 4.1 establishes straightforward equivalence up to constant shift under softmax invariance; sampler design (Eq. 9) primarily empirically motivated rather than theoretically derived
Evaluation limited to automatic metrics without human evaluation; no analysis of failure cases, systematic error patterns, or qualitative comparison of when/why SMOOTHIE outperforms alternatives
Critical issue: Code availability URL is blank ('The code is available at .'), undermining reproducibility despite comprehensive hyperparameter documentation
Experimental scope constrained to ~100M parameter models with relatively short sequences (max 512); scalability to larger models and longer sequences unexplored
Pre-trained embedding quality directly impacts performance (Appendix F: GloVe significantly underperforms BERT), suggesting method bounded by upstream representations
